entries.title: Scenarios for future banking: implications for profitability, liquidity and solvency
entries.description: Who will perform banking’s core functions a decade from now, and how will risks and profitability evolve? Our framework structures expert judgement rather than forecasts.

entries.title: Prewar US business cycles under uncertainty: reconstructing quarterly GDP before 1947
entries.description: Official quarterly US GDP estimates begin in 1947; earlier quarterly histories must be reconstructed using annual benchmarks and historical indicators. To investigate uncertainty in these reconstructions, this paper systematically compares specifications drawn from the literature for reconstructing quarterly GDP during 1919–1946. The comparison evaluates predictions on concealed postwar quarters and separates variation across specifications from coefficient uncertainty within a model.

entries.title: Building AI on credit: structures and spillovers

entries.title: Chokepoints in global supply chains: lessons from rare earths and hard disk drives
entries.description: Concentration and limited substitutability can turn the efficiency gains from global supply chains into vulnerabilities. However, the consequences of chokepoints depend on their underlying nature.

entries.title: News shocks and inflation:  theory and evidence from  large oil discoveries
entries.description: We study how news shocks affect inflation in open economies, using large oil and gas discoveries with realized production lags of at least five years as observable news about future output. Panel local projections show that discoveries raise core consumer prices over the subsequent decade, with about half the increase occurring prior to extraction.

entries.title: Bank liquidity regulation and the growth of private credit
entries.description: We study the role of bank liquidity regulation in the growth of private credit. Following the introduction of the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), private credit increases significantly more in U.S. counties with a larger footprint of banks subject to the LCR or of LCR banks with greater initial liquidity shortfalls.
